session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about

suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants shared names, ages, and UK locations (Birmingham, North East, Leeds, rural Scotland, Edinburgh). No substantive themes emerged yet. The moderator closed with a grounding question about favourite hangout spots with male friends, designed to ease participants into concrete, personal territory before moving toward food-related topics.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening was straightforward scene-setting: establish comfort, frame the session as conversational rather than interrogative, and use a low-stakes warm-up question to generate early participation. All five participants introduced themselves voluntarily without prompting, suggesting good initial engagement. The transition question about hangout spaces was well-pitched — specific and personal enough to invite genuine answers without being threatening.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the relationship between choice, familiarity, and social infrastructure across different settings. A productive tension emerged between urban participants who have options but default to habit, and Will's rural experience where the environment dictates the social experience entirely. The group converged on 'flexibility' as a value — not necessarily exercised, but meaningful as a latent possibility. Food appeared briefly as a functional, incidental backdrop to socialising rather than a deliberate consideration.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was ensuring all five voices entered before the section closed. Ibrahim and Amir engaged immediately and developed a genuine exchange; Will's rural contrast arrived organically and reframed the conversation productively. Two direct interventions were needed to bring in David and Isaiah, both of whom responded well once addressed. The approach of letting the Ibrahim–Amir–Will thread develop before interrupting was correct — it generated the flexibility theme that gave the later contributions something to orient against.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the distinction between habitual eating and genuine food choice — specifically whether consuming meat constitutes an active decision or simply an unexamined default. A productive tension emerged between Amir's position (considered preference) and Isaiah and Will's more honest acknowledgement of non-engagement with alternatives. David and Ibrahim occupied a middle ground: aware of alternatives, indifferent rather than opposed. The group converged on 'not thinking about it' as the dominant mode, with 'choice' reframed as a spectrum rather than binary.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was letting the Isaiah–Amir–Will philosophical exchange develop without interruption — it generated the section's sharpest conceptual distinction organically. Both moderator interventions were targeted: lifting Isaiah's framing into a group question, then drawing in David and Ibrahim once the core tension was established. David responded substantively unprompted after direct address; Ibrahim gave a thinner, more noncommittal answer. The transition question about gender was well-timed — the habitual/choice thread had reached natural resolution and needed a new stimulus.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section extended the habit/choice tension from Section 2 into explicitly gendered territory. The group moved through three linked ideas: that meat preferences are conditioned rather than freely chosen; that gendered norms are visible precisely because breaking them carries social cost (the 'salad moment'); and that most participants had been actively choosing not to interrogate whether they'd want the same thing absent that pressure. David's philosophical challenge — that no 'pure' preference exists beneath social shaping — was ultimately conceded as a deflection.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main tasks were reintroducing gender explicitly after the habit thread resolved, and converting abstract acknowledgement into concrete stakes via the salad scenario. Both moves worked — David and Isaiah, who had been peripheral, delivered the section's sharpest contributions once the scenario gave them something specific to respond to. Holding back during the Amir–Ibrahim exchange was correct; it generated the 'drifting vs. choosing' distinction organically. The final push toward practical consequences was well-timed but arrived at section close, leaving it as the next section's opening question.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened the habit/choice tension into two distinct barrier types: infrastructural (Will's rural logistics) versus social-as-default (Isaiah, Amir, Ibrahim). The more generative move was Isaiah's mid-section shift — from 'it's a choice' to 'I'm calling it a choice to avoid sitting with the fact I haven't questioned it' — which drew Amir and Ibrahim into honest self-assessment. The closing thread explored whether naming the barrier, without changing behaviour, constitutes any meaningful shift.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were: letting the Will–David exchange resolve without interruption, then using it to bring in the three silent participants; and directly confronting Isaiah's earlier framing with his new one, which produced the section's sharpest self-reflection. Both worked. Ibrahim needed a direct address late to contribute substantively — he arrived at a useful position but likely needed prompting earlier. The transition question pivoting to 'what would make plant-based food appealing' was well-timed once the barrier taxonomy felt complete.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on what would actually shift plant-based eating from 'statement' to normal — and whether the barriers are structural (infrastructure, visibility in small places) or social-psychological (the unacknowledged default status of meat). A productive tension emerged between waiting-for-permission versus just-doing-it approaches to norm change. The section's sharpest movement was Amir's gradual acknowledgement that his stated uncertainty about preference may itself be a form of knowing — comfort preferred over discomfort, dressed as genuine ambiguity.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were: surfacing the Will–Ibrahim structural-versus-philosophical tension for the group rather than resolving it, then using that as an entry point for the three quieter participants. Drilling into Amir's preference/performance distinction in the final exchange was the most productive intervention — the follow-up question about what 'actually preferring it' would look like unlocked his clearest self-reflection of the session. David's unsolicited challenge to Amir did much of that work; holding back and letting it develop was correct.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: The closing section produced a recursive layer of self-disclosure: participants catching themselves using their own framings — uncertainty, clarity, logistics — as shields against genuine accountability. The section's sharpest movement was a convergence on 'comfort as the actual preference,' stripped of justificatory scaffolding. Will's infrastructure argument was both validated and voluntarily complicated by Will himself, producing a three-way acknowledgement that different barrier types can serve identical avoidance functions.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were a short open invitation to any unfinished thoughts, then a targeted redirect to the three quieter participants once the Isaiah–Amir exchange ran. Both were light-touch and correct — the Isaiah–Amir thread required no steering and produced the session's most candid self-reflection. Will, David, and Ibrahim were addressed directly but without pressure; Will responded substantively. David and Ibrahim had not yet spoken by the transcript's end — a gap not yet resolved.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. We've got about 45 minutes together, and we're going to be talking about your food choices and opinions. It'll be recorded for research purposes, so just a heads up on that. The main thing to know is that there are genuinely no right or wrong answers here — I'm not looking for anything in particular, I just want to hear what you actually think and what your actual experiences are. So try not to overthink things, just speak freely. And this is meant to feel more like a conversation than an interview — you don't have to take turns or wait to be asked, just jump in if something connects with what someone else is saying or if you've got something to add. The only thing I'd ask is that you're respectful of each other and try to keep individual answers reasonably brief so everyone gets a chance to speak. Okay, let's get going — let's start by going around and saying your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham. West Midlands. Twenty years old.

Yeah, I'm Ibrahim. I'm from the North East, urban area. I'm twenty-four. 

*pauses slightly*

Good to meet you all.
Right, I'm Isaiah. I'm from Leeds, so Yorkshire and the Humber. I'm twenty-six. Good to meet you lot as well.
Right, I'm Will. I'm from rural Scotland — quite a bit more quiet than what you lot are used to, I reckon. I'm twenty-nine. Good to meet you all too.
Right, I'm David. I'm from urban Scotland — Edinburgh area, so yeah, not quite as quiet as Will's patch. I'm twenty-seven. Good to meet everyone.

Great, good to have everyone here — Amir, Ibrahim, Isaiah, Will, and David. Right, let's get into it. I want to start with something fairly easy and specific. Think about where you tend to spend time with your male friends — could be a particular pub, a park, a gym, wherever it is for you. What's your favourite place in your city or area to hang out with the lads, and what is it about that place that makes it work for you?

There's this spot near the quayside — you know, down by the river. It's got a few bars and restaurants around it, pretty lively on weekends. We usually end up at one of the pubs there, nothing fancy. I think it just works because it's central, easy to get to, and there's always something going on — live music sometimes, people about. You can grab a drink, have a laugh, doesn't matter if you're there for two hours or five. And honestly, the food's decent too if you're hungry — they do good burgers, steaks, that kind of thing. That matters when you've had a few and want something substantial, you know?

Yeah, that makes sense. We've got similar spots around Birmingham — like the Bullring's got that vibe, loads going on, but honestly I'm more into the quieter places. Cannon Hill Park's where we actually hang out proper, you know? It's not just about getting drinks and that. Like, you can actually have a conversation without shouting over everyone. And yeah, the food thing Ibrahim mentioned — I get that. When you're hungry you want something decent, a proper meal. But I think for me it's more about just being able to chill and actually talk to your mates rather than just being in a mad busy spot. Nothing against it, just depends what you're in the mood for.

Yeah, I hear you on that. Cannon Hill sounds good for that. But I think the quayside's got both, to be honest. Like, yeah, it gets busy and there's energy, but it's not chaotic — you can still sit down, have proper conversations. It's not like you're forced to be shouting at each other. And that's kind of the point of it for us, I think. You've got the option, you know? Some nights you want that buzz going on around you, other nights you just want to chill with a pint and talk about stuff. The fact that it's got the food, the bars, the space to actually sit and be with your mates — that's why it works. You don't have to choose between one thing or the other.

Fair point, yeah. I suppose I was thinking more like chaotic busy, but you're right — having options is the thing, isn't it? You can pick how you want the night to go depending on what you're after. Cannon Hill's quieter so it's naturally more that way, but what you're saying about having the buzz there if you want it but also being able to chat properly... that does work. I get that. You get the flexibility, basically.

Yeah, that flexibility thing — that's the bit that's different where I am, really. Like, there's maybe one or two pubs that work, and that's kind of it. You go there because it's the only option, not because you're choosing between a few different vibes, you know? You can't just decide halfway through the night "oh, I fancy somewhere quieter" or "let's go find a spot with a bit more going on." It's what you've got.

Don't get me wrong, it's alright. The people are good, everyone knows everyone. But there's no flexibility about it. You're not picking how the night's going to feel — the place kind of determines it for you. Whereas what you two are saying, it sounds like you've actually got... options. You can tailor what you're doing depending on what you want. That's a different thing entirely.

That's a really different picture, Will — having the place make the decision for you rather than the other way round. David, Isaiah, we haven't heard from you two yet — whereabouts do you tend to end up with your mates?

Yeah, so I'm similar to Will in some ways, I think. I mean, Edinburgh's got loads going on, so it's not quite the same constraint he's talking about, but... I don't know, I'm not really one for planning it out that much. I tend to just end up at the same few spots, if I'm honest. There's a couple of pubs near Leith Walk that mates and I gravitate towards, and we just kind of go there because we know it, not necessarily because we've weighed up all the options, you know? 

Will's right though — there's something about having choice and then there's something about just... knowing where you're going. I think both have their thing. Like, the spots we go to aren't fancy, they're just familiar. You know the people behind the bar, you know roughly what you're getting. And that works fine for just hanging out and having a laugh with the lads.

But yeah, I do have more options than Will's describing, so I guess if I got bored of Leith Walk I could try somewhere else. Whereas if you've only got the one or two places, that's... that's just the reality of where you live, isn't it?

Right, yeah — that's fair. You've got the option there if you want it, even if you don't always use it. That's different from what I'm saying. Like, you could get bored and go somewhere new if you fancied it. I can't really do that.

And I'm not saying familiarity's bad — that bit David said about knowing the people behind the bar and what you're getting, that's exactly it for me too. That's comfortable. But it's not the same as choosing to be familiar with a place because you like it, you know? It's more just... this is where everyone goes because it's the only place that works. You're not weighing it up. There's no "well, I could go somewhere else" sitting in the back of your head, even if you don't act on it.
Isaiah, we haven't heard from you yet — whereabouts do you end up with your mates in Leeds?

Yeah, so I'm a bit like David, I reckon. There's this spot — couple of bars and a gym actually near where I live, so we end up there a lot just because it's easy, you know? It's not really a conscious choice most of the time, just... that's where we go. But I think what you're all saying about having options — I get that. Leeds has got loads of places, so like, if we got bored we could go somewhere else, but we just don't really bother most of the time.

I think the familiar thing is... it's comfortable, isn't it? You know what you're getting, you're not arsed with trying somewhere new every time you want to hang out. But Will's point about only having one or two places — that does sound different. Like, at least I've got the option there if I wanted it, even if I don't think about it much.

And yeah, the food thing — we usually grab something while we're there or after. It's not like we're planning a meal out or anything, just whatever's available and decent. Does the job.

Interesting how that varies. Let's shift to something connected — thinking about your day-to-day now, how do you actually decide what to eat? Like, what's driving that for you?
